frase_gancho.texto: The colossal water goddess who traveled by train.

puente_narrativo.texto: Notice her outstretched hands. Now step into a house in the city, where a similar figure pours water from a wall, and below it opens a paradise where everyone swims, sings, and plays.

guion_corto.texto: This stone woman stands more than three meters tall and weighs about sixteen tons. She is Chalchiuhtlicue, “she of the jade skirt,” the goddess of flowing water: rivers, lakes, springs. That name is Mexica; the name the people of Teotihuacán gave her is unknown to us. Notice her enormous rectangular headdress, her round ear ornaments, her beaded necklace, and her skirt, and above all her hands, stretched out in front of her, as if she were offering something or letting water fall. Everything about her is straight and firm, like a block that breathes. She was found near the Pyramid of the Moon, and in 1888 she was taken to Mexico City. A goddess for a city that depended on its springs.

guion_largo.texto:
Her move was almost as famous as she is. In 1888, the archaeologist Leopoldo Batres arranged to bring her to the museum on Moneda Street, in the historic center of the capital. She traveled by train, and according to the museum label the stone, of about sixteen tons, had to wait five months outside the old museum before going in. Imagine the scene: a block of more than sixteen tons arriving in the city at the end of the nineteenth century.

The people of Teotihuacán moved her long before, and without mules, without wheels, and without metal. They had no pack animals, so the work was done by people, with ropes, logs, and patience. The stone was carved with other, harder stones and with sand and water, which wear it down little by little. To think that this block was worked in that way, more than fifteen hundred years ago, helps us understand what it meant to the city: a work of enormous collective effort.

Here there is a connection with the museum entrance. The stone giant on the esplanade, the one everyone calls Tláloc, looks very much like this woman: the same almost square block, the same geometric forms, the same style without ornament. That is why several specialists think that it, too, could be a water goddess. They are two of the largest sculptures of ancient Mexico, and both made a journey to the capital: this one in 1888, by train; the other in 1964, on a giant trailer.

The name “Chalchiuhtlicue” comes from the Mexica, who lived a thousand years later. For them she was the companion of Tláloc, the goddess who bathed newborns: in the ritual that followed birth, the midwife invoked her name while washing the baby. Some researchers prefer to speak of a Great Goddess of Teotihuacán, a powerful female figure linked to water, the earth, and caves, who appears in murals and sculptures under different names depending on who interprets her.

The Mexica also told that Chalchiuhtlicue ruled one of the eras before our own, the Fourth Sun, which ended in a great flood, and that the people of that time turned into fish. For them, water gave life and could also take it away. If you remember the fish vessel you saw in the previous hall, it is the same idea, told in a different way: people and water, always together.

Teotihuacán rose in a valley of irregular rainfall, beside springs, and its inhabitants channeled the San Juan River so that it would cross the city. They made use of every drop. A goddess like this was not an ornament: she was the way of asking the water to keep coming. And the hands, stretched out in front, could be receiving offerings or pouring water; the sculpture does not make it clear, and that ambiguity is part of its power.

Why is she so rigid? The sculptors of Teotihuacán preferred simple forms: flat planes, right angles, faces that look like masks. They did not seek to portray anyone, but to show something divine and stable. That is why the lines of this figure do not move, and why, even though she weighs as much as a house, she seems to float.

Follow the trail of water through this hall: you will see it in a mural where it flows down from a mountain, in conch shells that sound like rain, and, farther on, in the god whom the Mexica placed beside Huitzilopochtli at the top of the Templo Mayor. Rain unites the halls.

texto.Origin: Teotihuacán, State of Mexico (Plaza of the Moon, in front of the Pyramid of the Moon)
texto.Dimensions: 3.16 m high x 1.65 m wide x 1.65 m thick
texto.Discovery: Moved in 1888 to the former National Museum, on Moneda Street, by Leopoldo Batres

texto.pregunta: Myth: The people of Teotihuacán called this goddess Chalchiuhtlicue.
texto.respuesta: Reality: That name is Mexica and came a thousand years later; we do not know what the goddess was called by those who sculpted her.
